theme: The river of life; the new land, new creation anticipated
readingInstruction: Read Ezekiel 47:1-48:35. A river flows from the temple and turns a desert into a place of life, and the land is divided among the twelve tribes, ending with a city whose name is “The LORD Is There.” Read the river carefully, and notice what it does.
settingTheScene: This is the last vision of Ezekiel’s book. After the return of the glory, a river flows from the threshold of the temple. It grows deeper as it moves toward the Dead Sea, and wherever it goes, it brings life. Then the land is divided fairly among the tribes, including foreigners who live among them. The book ends with the new name of the city, a promise that answers the sorrow of the first part: the glory had left, and now God is present forever.
observation: “Behold, water was issuing from below the threshold of the temple toward the east” (47:1).
“Again he measured a thousand, and led me through the water, water that was to the ankles… to the knees… to the loins” (47:3-4).
“It was a river that I could not pass through, for the water had risen. It was deep enough to swim in” (47:5).
“This water flows toward the eastern region and goes down into the Arabah, and enters the Sea. When the water flows into the Sea, the water of the Sea will become fresh” (47:8).
“Swarms of creatures will live wherever the river goes… everything will live where the river goes” (47:9).
“On the banks, on both sides of the river, there will grow all kinds of trees for food. Their leaves will not wither, nor their fruit fail” (47:12).
“You shall divide it for an inheritance among yourselves and for the sojourners who reside among you” (47:22).
“And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There” (48:35).
interpretation:
The river begins as a trickle under the temple threshold. Following the guide, Ezekiel wades in at the ankles, then the knees, then the waist, and then it is a river he cannot cross. The image is of overflowing, increasing grace. A small source from the presence of God becomes a flood of life. And the direction is downhill into the Judean desert, to the Dead Sea, the most lifeless place on earth. The salty water becomes fresh, and fish swarm there. Fishermen stand on the shore. The river brings life even to death.

On the banks, fruit trees grow every month. The leaves do not wither. The fruit is for food, and the leaves for healing. And the reason is stated: “because the water for them flows from the sanctuary.” All life flows from the presence of God. This is Eden restored.

The rest of the chapter deals with the boundaries of the land and the division among the tribes. Notable is the inclusion of the sojourners: “You shall allot it for an inheritance among yourselves and for the foreigners who reside among you and have fathered children among you. You shall treat them as native-born Israelites.” The covenant community is extended to include outsiders.

Chapter 48 lists the tribal portions, each as a strip running east to west, with the holy portion at the center. The city has twelve gates, named for the twelve tribes. And the book ends with its last line: “The name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There.” It is a fitting end for a book that began with God’s glory leaving. The glory is back, and it will not leave again.

For the Christian, the river is a picture of the Spirit and the gospel, flowing from the presence of God to the dead places of the world. It finds its fulfillment in Revelation 22.
connection: John 7:37-39 says that Jesus invited anyone who is thirsty to come, and that out of his heart will flow rivers of living water, referring to the Spirit. Revelation 22:1-2 describes the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on both banks, “and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.” Revelation 21:3 says, “The dwelling place of God is with man.” Revelation 21:12-14 describes the city with twelve gates. Ephesians 2:19 says that Gentiles are no longer strangers but fellow citizens.
application:
Think of a “Dead Sea” in your life or community. Pray for the river of God’s life to reach it.

Ask whether the grace you have received is deeper than “ankle-deep.” Wade further in.

Welcome a stranger into your community, as the tribes were told to welcome the sojourners.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to let the river of his life flow into dead places in you.
Thank Jesus, the source of living water.
Pray for a place that is barren.
